newsitem.title: POLAND: Embattled Polish army chief clings to post.
newsitem.headline: Embattled Polish army chief clings to post.

text.p: Poland's armed forces chief Tadeusz Wilecki, accused by critics of undermining full civilian control of the military which is a key to NATO entry, on Wednesday denied press reports he was about to quit.
Asked to comment on newspaper reports that his removal was close, General Wilecki dismissed them as nonsense and told a news conference he would not stand down for now.

Controversy has swirled around Wilecki since a September 1994 dinner at the Drawsko training ground when then president Lech Walesa reportedly asked generals what they thought of civilian Defence Minister Piotr Kolodziejczyk, then sacked him.

Some officials of NATO countries and domestic critics saw the episode as a joint move by Walesa and the general staff to sideline the defence ministry and said Poland had to perfect parliamentary civilian control before joining the pact.
This prompted a reform last year which strengthened the role of parliament's defence committee and altered the general staff.

Defenders of Walesa and Wilecki argued that continuity was essential for development of the defence sector and this could better be provided by the staff and the presidency, with its five-year term and responsibility for national security, than by the fast-changing cabinets since the 1989 fall of communism.

Wilecki repeated at Wednesday's news conference in Warsaw that the general staff had provided stability in a time of political change and Poland's army had won praise from NATO officers and become a model for other Warsaw Pact countries.
"I say all this because here and there voices are cropping up saying it is these soldiers, it is this chief of staff, who is standing in the way of our growing closer to NATO," he said.
He said many accounts of the Drawsko affair were false and promised to invite journalists soon to hear the full story.

Wilecki, who has long been disliked by the ex-communists dominating the Polish government since 1993, has been exposed since ex-communist Aleksander Kwasniewski beat Walesa in late 1995 presidential polls.

The head of the ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance's (SLD) parliamentary caucus, Jerzy Szmajdzinski, said on Wednesday it was time for the general to go as he had been the favourite of the former political establishment.
"General Tadeusz Wilecki's time has passed," PAP news agency quoted Szmajdzinski as telling a news conference. He added that it was not up to his party to remove the general.
Poland's Gazeta Wyborcza daily reported earlier this week that Wilecki was expected to resign soon but that Kwasniewski had so far resisted calls for his dismissal.
